paragraphs: A world model predicts how an environment changes in response to actions. Adapting such a model becomes difficult when a new environment uses different actions and offers only limited opportunities for interaction. AdaWorld addresses this problem by incorporating action information during pretraining, without requiring explicit action labels for the videos used to learn that information.

The method extracts latent actions from videos through self-supervised learning. These learned representations capture important transitions between frames. An autoregressive world model then uses the latent actions to condition its predictions, learning how visual changes relate to this internal action representation. This gives subsequent adaptation a foundation that already connects action information with changes in the environment.

The authors report that this approach supports transfer and learning of new actions with limited interactions and finetuning. Across multiple environments, AdaWorld achieves superior simulation quality and visual planning performance in the reported experiments. The findings support learning action-related structure before adaptation as a way to make world models more reusable across environments with different action systems.
icml-2025-adaworld-learning-adaptable-wo.tldr: AdaWorld learns latent actions from videos during pretraining to help world models adapt to new environments with limited interaction and finetuning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve decisions using previously collected experience. A central risk is selecting unfamiliar actions whose apparent value is misleading. Behavior regularization addresses this by keeping the learned policy close to a reference behavior policy. BDPO extends this approach to diffusion policies, where actions emerge through a sequence of generative transitions.

The technical challenge is expressing the behavior constraint for this more elaborate policy representation. BDPO analytically calculates the Kullback–Leibler regularization through accumulated differences between reverse-time transition kernels along the diffusion trajectory. This connects the policy-level constraint to the individual transitions that generate an action, making regularization usable within diffusion-based policy optimization.

The authors incorporate this calculation into an efficient actor–critic algorithm operating on two timescales, described as producing the optimal policy while respecting the behavior constraint. Evaluations on synthetic two-dimensional tasks and continuous-control tasks from D4RL support its effectiveness and superior performance in those settings. The contribution combines the expressive action modeling of diffusion policies with an explicit mechanism for restraining departures from reference behavior.
icml-2025-behavior-regularized-diffusion.tldr: BDPO makes behavior regularization tractable for diffusion policies by calculating its KL penalty through the transitions that generate actions.

paragraphs: Generating a long video often means producing one clip after another, using earlier frames to guide each new clip. Existing autoregressive video diffusion models repeatedly process these shared conditioning frames. When the retained context grows over successive clips, this repeated work becomes especially expensive, with the abstract describing quadratic computational growth in the autoregression step.

Ca2-VDM changes feature computation so that information flows in one direction. This causal organization allows features for conditioning frames to be computed during earlier generation steps, stored, and reused in later steps. The method also shares the stored cache across denoising steps, addressing the storage burden that would otherwise accompany caching throughout diffusion generation.

These two components tackle related costs: causal computation removes redundant processing of past frames, while cache sharing reduces the associated memory burden. Extensive experiments report faster generation alongside state-of-the-art quantitative and qualitative video results. The findings indicate that restructuring how previous context is computed and retained can improve generation efficiency while also supporting strong video quality in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-ca2-vdm-efficient-autoregressi.tldr: Ca2-VDM accelerates autoregressive video generation by reusing causally computed frame features and sharing their cache across denoising steps.

paragraphs: Clinical trials with small control groups can benefit from control observations collected elsewhere, but differences between data sources can bias treatment comparisons. This paper studies that problem for censored survival outcomes, where some event times are not fully observed. Its target is the difference between treatment-specific restricted mean survival times, which summarizes survival over a restricted time horizon.

The proposed estimator addresses two forms of mismatch. Doubly robust estimation adjusts for shifts in measured covariates between the trial and external data. A DR-Learner then supports selective borrowing by identifying outcome drift, allowing the method to use comparable external controls. Machine learning can estimate survival curves and detect these differences without imposing strict parametric forms.

The authors describe the resulting estimator as more efficient than estimators using only trial data while mitigating bias from external observations. Simulations and an application involving Galcanezumab for migraine headaches illustrate the framework. The methodological contribution is to combine adjustment with selective borrowing, so that additional controls contribute information according to their comparability rather than merely their availability.
icml-2025-doubly-protected-estimation-fo.tldr: The proposed survival estimator combines covariate adjustment and selective borrowing to improve trial efficiency while mitigating bias from external controls.

paragraphs: Removing an unwanted concept from a text-to-image model requires changing what it generates without broadly damaging its capabilities. EraseAnything addresses this challenge in newer systems that combine flow-based generation with transformer architectures. The authors argue that these architectural changes limit the transfer of erasure techniques designed for earlier text-to-image models.

EraseAnything formulates the task as a bi-level optimization problem, coupling two levels of optimization. It uses LoRA-based parameter tuning together with a regularizer on attention maps to selectively suppress unwanted activations. A self-contrastive learning strategy is intended to protect performance on concepts unrelated to the removal target, making preservation part of the method rather than only an evaluation concern.

The paper presents the approach as the first specifically developed for concept erasure in this newer flow-based framework. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of erasure tasks. These findings support adapting the optimization and preservation mechanisms to the model architecture, with the reported success covering selective concept removal as well as the goal of maintaining broader generative quality.
icml-2025-eraseanything-enabling-concept.tldr: EraseAnything adapts concept erasure to flow-based text-to-image transformers using targeted parameter updates, attention regularization, and self-contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Safety constraints based on average cumulative cost can underrepresent rare events with severe consequences. Extreme Value Policy Optimization, or EVO, focuses on these tail events in constrained reinforcement learning. It uses Extreme Value Theory to model extreme reward and cost samples, with the aim of reducing violations that expectation-based objectives can overlook.

EVO introduces an extreme-quantile optimization objective that explicitly accounts for the cost distribution's tail. It also prioritizes extreme samples during replay, strengthening the training signal from events that occur rarely but matter greatly. These components address both what the policy optimizes and how strongly unusual experiences influence its updates.

The theoretical analysis bounds expected constraint violations during policy updates and establishes strict satisfaction at a zero-violation quantile level. That stated guarantee is tied to this quantile condition. The authors also show lower violation probability than expectation-based methods and lower variance than quantile regression methods. Experiments report substantially fewer training-time violations while maintaining competitive policy performance, supporting tail-focused optimization as a useful approach to safer learning.
icml-2025-extreme-value-policy-optimizat.tldr: EVO targets extreme cost events through quantile optimization and prioritized replay, reducing observed constraint violations while retaining competitive policy performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how transformers discover computations when the structure of their training data can be controlled. The authors introduce hierarchical filtering for sequence models built on trees. Filtering lets them adjust the range of positional correlations, creating a setting in which dependencies at different distances can be examined separately.

They train standard encoder-only transformers on root classification and masked language modeling. In this controlled setting, they find evidence that the networks can approximate the exact inference algorithm. During training, correlations over larger distances enter the learned computation sequentially, corresponding to progressively higher levels of the underlying hierarchy.

Comparisons of attention maps under different filtering settings, together with probes of encoder levels, support reconstruction of correlations at successive length scales. The authors relate these observations to a plausible implementation of exact inference within the transformer architecture. The result is evidence about how structured computation can emerge during learning: it connects training progression, internal representations, and known data structure without claiming that the proposed implementation is uniquely established.
icml-2025-how-transformers-learn-structu.tldr: Controlled tree-structured data reveal evidence that encoder transformers learn increasingly distant correlations and approximate an exact inference procedure.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction represents uncertainty with sets of possible outcomes. Cross-conformal prediction uses multiple data folds and was introduced to improve prediction-set width relative to split conformal prediction. This paper asks whether the statistical combination step can be improved further, producing smaller sets while retaining the coverage guarantees available for the existing methods.

The authors propose variants of both the original cross-conformal method and a simple modification of it. Their construction uses results on combining p-values more efficiently through exchangeability and randomization. The improvement therefore comes from how statistical evidence is combined, with the goal of extracting tighter prediction sets without weakening the corresponding theoretical protection.

The guarantees require careful interpretation: the modified existing method has a marginal coverage lower bound of 1 − 2α, while the original method's stated bound also includes a correction involving sample size and fold count. The new variants preserve these respective guarantees; the abstract does not upgrade them to 1 − α. Simulations confirm the theoretical findings and reveal tradeoffs, supporting improved set efficiency within the established coverage framework.
icml-2025-improving-the-statistical-effi.tldr: New cross-conformal variants combine p-values more efficiently to shrink prediction sets while preserving the existing methods' coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: Decision-making systems may encounter diverse tasks that were unknown during training. This paper proposes learning a committee of policies so that, with high probability, at least one member is near-optimal for a task encountered during execution. This shifts the learning target toward a collection that covers task diversity.

The authors show that the committee-learning problem is generally inapproximable, then develop two practical approaches. One provides approximation and task sample complexity guarantees when tasks are low-dimensional. The other uses gradient-based learning and is intended as a more general practical solution. The paper also establishes a sample complexity bound for learning from only a few examples.

Experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World report better training, generalization, and few-shot learning performance than state-of-the-art multi-task, meta-learning, and task-clustering baselines, often by a substantial margin. The theoretical and empirical contributions have distinct scopes: low-dimensional structure enables the stated approximation guarantees, while the broader gradient-based method offers a practical route to building committees. Together, they support policy diversity as a means of preparing for varied future tasks.
icml-2025-learning-policy-committees-for.tldr: Policy committees aim to cover diverse future tasks with a near-optimal member, combining conditional theoretical guarantees with strong empirical personalization results.

paragraphs: Large language models can enrich node representations before those representations enter a graph neural network. Although this combination has shown promise, the paper asks how the two components interact internally. Its focus is the mechanism through which language-derived information becomes useful to graph learning, rather than performance alone.

The authors construct a synthetic graph dataset whose causal relationships can be controlled. This allows semantic relationships to be manipulated in a setting designed for causal analysis. They then apply interchange interventions to investigate the behavior of the language-model enhancer and the graph neural network, using controlled interventions to examine their underlying computations.

The analysis informs a plug-and-play optimization module intended to improve information transfer between the two components. Experiments across multiple datasets and models validate the proposed module. The contribution thus connects a controlled investigation with a practical modification: observations about internal interaction guide how enhanced node information is passed into graph learning. The supplied findings support the usefulness of that analysis-driven design across the evaluated model and dataset combinations.
icml-2025-llm-enhancers-for-gnns-an-anal.tldr: Controlled causal interventions reveal how LLM-enhanced node features interact with GNNs and inform a module that improves their information transfer.

paragraphs: An agent that chooses its own goals must decide where further practice will produce the most learning. This becomes difficult when the goal space is large and changes over time. MAGELLAN addresses this problem for language-model agents trained with online reinforcement learning by helping them predict their own competence and learning progress.

The framework learns these predictions during interaction. It captures semantic relationships between goals so that knowledge about some goals can inform estimates for others. This generalization supports more sample-efficient progress estimation and adaptation as the goal space evolves. It also addresses the reliance of earlier approaches on extensive sampling or fragile, expert-defined goal groupings.

In the reported interactive environment, MAGELLAN improves both learning-progress prediction efficiency and goal prioritization. Among the methods compared, it is the only one that enables full mastery of the large, evolving goal space. That finding is specific to the evaluated setting, while supporting the broader idea that learned self-assessment can help agents organize their own curricula when enumerating and testing every possible goal would be costly.
icml-2025-magellan-metacognitive-predict.tldr: MAGELLAN helps LLM agents choose productive goals by learning to predict their own competence and progress across related goals.

paragraphs: Language models can generate mathematical solutions for their own training, but producing more data does not automatically produce better reasoning. The paper identifies ineffective exploration across reasoning stages as a source of spurious correlations in self-generated data. MARGE addresses this problem by changing how the model explores the reasoning process.

Its hit-guided exploration systematically examines intermediate states taken from self-generated solutions. These partial reasoning states become opportunities to explore, helping the method cover more of the solution process and improve credit assignment. Credit assignment concerns which parts of a reasoning trajectory should receive responsibility for its outcome, making intermediate exploration relevant to what the model learns from its generated work.

The authors report improvements in both single-shot accuracy and exploration diversity. This combination matters because alignment methods can face a tradeoff between producing a strong individual answer and retaining varied exploration. MARGE's stated results suggest that guided exploration can mitigate that tradeoff, supporting the use of self-generated training data as a scalable resource for improving mathematical reasoning.
icml-2025-marge-improving-math-reasoning.tldr: MARGE explores intermediate states of self-generated math solutions to improve credit assignment, single-shot accuracy, and exploration diversity.

paragraphs: Language-model training corpora mix sources with different styles, domains, and quality levels. Metadata Conditioning then Cooldown, or MeCo, gives the model extra cues about those differences during pretraining. It initially supplies metadata, such as a source URL, alongside text, then finishes with a cooldown phase containing ordinary text alone.

The cooldown enables normal operation without metadata after training. Across models ranging from 600 million to 8 billion parameters and several training corpora, the authors report accelerated pretraining. In one example, a 1.6-billion-parameter model matches standard pretraining's downstream performance while using 33% less data. The method is described as simple and adding no computational overhead.

Metadata also provides a way to steer outputs at inference time. The paper reports that real or invented source cues can influence behavior, including reducing harmful generations or improving common-knowledge task performance in the demonstrated examples. Model-generated topics can serve as metadata too. These findings suggest that training-time context about text sources can improve learning efficiency while creating additional handles for controlling the resulting model.
icml-2025-metadata-conditioning-accelera.tldr: MeCo uses metadata during pretraining followed by text-only cooldown to improve data efficiency and enable metadata-based output steering.

paragraphs: A continually learning model needs to express uncertainty as it moves through a sequence of tasks. Standard conformal prediction offers coverage guarantees when samples are exchangeable, meaning their ordering does not change their joint statistical behavior. Sequential task learning violates that premise, and limited access to earlier task data also makes constructing calibration data difficult.

CPCL is a conformal-prediction-based method designed for this setting. The authors analyze an oracle prediction interval and establish an asymptotic coverage guarantee for their method. This is a large-sample guarantee, preserving an important distinction from an unrestricted claim of exact coverage at every stage of continual learning.

The paper also identifies a connection between prediction-interval length and forgetting, linking uncertainty quantification with the loss of previously learned capabilities. Experiments on simulated and real data empirically support the method's validity. Together, the results address both the reliability of uncertainty estimates and their relationship to a characteristic challenge of continual learning, while adapting calibration to a setting where ordinary exchangeability and ready access to past observations are unavailable.
icml-2025-model-uncertainty-quantificati.tldr: CPCL adapts conformal uncertainty estimation to continual learning, proving asymptotic coverage and connecting prediction-interval length with forgetting.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for combinatorial optimization have different strengths, so the best solver overall may not be the best choice for every problem instance. This paper finds complementary performance among existing solvers and develops a framework for coordinating them. Its goal is to route each instance to the solver or solvers most suited to it.

The framework has three components: extracting instance features, building a selection model, and choosing a selection strategy. The authors assemble several strong existing neural solvers as alternatives and investigate different implementations of these components. This makes instance-level selection the central mechanism for improving the combined system.

Experiments cover the Traveling Salesman Problem and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem. The composite solver outperforms the best individual neural solver with little additional time cost, with reported optimality-gap reductions of 0.88% on TSPLIB and 0.71% on CVRPLIB. These results show that complementary solver behavior can translate into practical gains when a selection mechanism assigns work effectively, making coordination a productive direction alongside improvements to individual solvers.
icml-2025-neural-solver-selection-for-co.tldr: Instance-level selection combines complementary neural solvers into a stronger optimization system with little additional runtime in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Training language models to use long contexts is difficult when naturally long documents are scarce. Simply synthesizing longer inputs does not necessarily provide a clear mechanism for teaching long-range dependencies. NExtLong constructs training sequences that require the model to distinguish relevant, distant context from intervening distractions.

The framework breaks a document into meta-chunks and inserts hard negative distractors retrieved from pretraining corpora between them. These additions extend the context while separating related parts of the original document. Because the inserted material is distracting, the model must identify which distant content belongs to the dependency it needs to follow.

Experiments report significant gains on HELMET and RULER over existing long-context synthesis approaches and leading models trained on non-synthetic long documents. The stated findings support reducing dependence on naturally long documents for long-context training. The contribution is a specific construction principle: artificial length becomes useful training pressure when relevant material is separated by challenging distractions, giving the model a reason to learn selective use of information across long distances.
icml-2025-nextlong-toward-effective-long.tldr: NExtLong interleaves document chunks with hard distractors to train long-range context use while reducing reliance on naturally long documents.

paragraphs: Weather forecasting must connect large-scale atmospheric behavior with detailed regional conditions. OneForecast addresses this within a graph neural network framework, targeting difficulties that include balancing global and regional resolution, preserving extreme-event detail, and modeling evolving dynamics. The approach organizes global and regional forecasting as a nested system.

Its multi-scale graph combines a dynamical-system perspective with multi-grid ideas. The target region receives a denser graph to capture fine local features. An adaptive messaging mechanism uses dynamic gates to integrate node and edge information, supporting more accurate extreme-event forecasts. For high-resolution regional predictions, a neural nested grid method aims to reduce information loss at regional boundaries.

The experiments report strong performance across global and regional scales and across short- and long-term forecasts, with particular strength on extreme events. The findings support the combination of multi-scale representation, adaptive information exchange, and regional nesting. These components address connected aspects of the forecasting problem: retaining broad context, resolving local variation, and passing useful information into the region where greater detail is needed.
icml-2025-oneforecast-a-universal-framew.tldr: OneForecast combines multi-scale graphs, adaptive messaging, and nested regional grids to support global and detailed regional weather prediction.

paragraphs: Representations inside a language model change as they move through its layers. This paper studies those changes using zigzag persistence, a mathematical framework from topological data analysis. The aim is to connect that framework to practical algorithms for examining the model as a connected sequence of transformations.

The authors introduce descriptors that track how topological features, expressed as holes of different dimensions, persist and evolve across layers. Following their full evolution provides information that separate layer measurements followed by aggregation can miss. The descriptors offer a statistical view of how prompts change their relative positions within the representation space as processing proceeds.

The paper demonstrates that these descriptors respond to differences between models and datasets, supporting their expressivity and practical applicability. As a downstream use, the authors derive a layer-pruning criterion from zigzag persistence and report results comparable to state-of-the-art methods. This connects a system-wide description of representation changes with a concrete model-simplification task, while retaining the emphasis on relationships across layers rather than isolated layer summaries.
icml-2025-persistent-topological-feature.tldr: Zigzag persistence tracks topological structure across language-model layers and supports a pruning criterion with results comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Guidance helps diffusion models generate outputs that match a condition, but the paper identifies a mismatch between common implementations and their theoretical justification. The authors prove that the scaled marginal distribution target used in that motivation is invalid and replace it with a valid objective based on a scaled joint distribution.

They then interpret established guidance implementations as approximations to an intractable optimal solution under a no-future-foresight constraint. This supplies a theoretical account of what practical guidance is approximating. From that analysis, they develop rectified gradient guidance, or REG, as an enhancement that can be incorporated into existing guidance methods.

Experiments in one and two dimensions show that REG more closely approximates the optimal solution than prior guidance techniques. Further evaluations on class-conditional ImageNet and text-to-image generation report consistent improvements in FID and Inception or CLIP scores across the tested settings when REG is added. The work connects a correction to the mathematical objective with a practical modification whose reported benefits extend from simple test settings to image generation.
icml-2025-reg-rectified-gradient-guidanc.tldr: REG corrects the theoretical objective behind diffusion guidance and improves existing guidance methods in the reported generation experiments.

paragraphs: A platform can manipulate an audit by giving a regulator different answers from those it gives ordinary users. Passing such an audit would not demonstrate that the platform changed its normal behavior. This paper studies how an auditor's prior knowledge of the platform's task can help prevent that form of manipulation.

The authors first show why reliance on public prior information, such as a public dataset, leaves an auditor vulnerable to being fooled. They then formally characterize conditions under which prior knowledge about the ground truth can prevent manipulation. The result makes the nature of the auditor's knowledge part of the auditing problem, rather than treating the audit data alone as sufficient protection.

Experiments on two standard datasets illustrate how much unfairness a platform can conceal before it is detected as malicious. These experiments complement the theoretical conditions by examining the boundary between hidden misconduct and detectable manipulation. The contribution is a framework for reasoning about fairness audits in the presence of strategic platforms, with protection tied to the stated conditions on prior knowledge.
icml-2025-robust-ml-auditing-using-prior.tldr: The paper characterizes when an auditor's prior ground-truth knowledge can prevent platforms from concealing unfair behavior through manipulated audit responses.

paragraphs: In symmetric constant-sum games with more than two players, an equilibrium does not necessarily protect a player against opponents using other equilibria or non-equilibrium strategies. This paper therefore studies a concrete performance objective: securing an expected payoff of C/n when n players share a total payoff of C.

The authors identify theoretical conditions under which achieving this equal-share objective is computationally tractable. They design efficient algorithms inspired by no-regret learning that provably achieve approximate equal share across several settings. Complementary lower bounds establish the sharpness of the theoretical results, clarifying the boundaries of what the algorithms can guarantee.

Experiments highlight worst-case scenarios in which meta-algorithms from prior state-of-the-art multiplayer systems fail to secure equal share, while the proposed algorithm succeeds. These results support equal share as a useful target for competitive play under the studied conditions. The guarantee concerns expected payoff and approximate attainment in the relevant settings, providing a principled objective for situations where equilibrium-based reasoning alone offers insufficient protection.
icml-2025-securing-equal-share-a-princip.tldr: The paper establishes conditions and efficient learning algorithms for securing approximately equal expected payoff in multiplayer symmetric constant-sum games.

paragraphs: Groups of users may try to influence a learning platform by coordinating changes to the data they submit. This paper studies the computations needed to organize such collective action. The central question is how a group can assess its likely influence and coordinate an implementable strategy using information available from observations.

The framework addresses two connected needs. First, a collective should estimate the effects of its intervention before acting, because altering its data may carry risks. Second, its coordination algorithm must depend on quantities that can be inferred from observed data. Together, these requirements connect prospective impact assessment with the practical information needed to carry out a coordinated intervention.

The authors provide a theoretical and algorithmic treatment and present experiments in a product-evaluation setting. The stated contribution is a framework for analyzing and implementing collective influence under these informational requirements. It makes the group's own computational problem explicit: participants need a way to reason about anticipated platform responses and translate those assessments into coordinated data changes before accepting the risks of action.
icml-2025-statistical-collusion-by-colle.tldr: The paper develops a framework for collectives to estimate and coordinate their influence on learning platforms through altered data submissions.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels. This paper considers an online setting in which examples arrive over time and feedback is incomplete: the true label becomes visible only when the prediction set includes it. The set chosen by the learner therefore also determines whether useful label feedback is available.

Document retrieval illustrates the problem. A user can identify the desired document only if it appears among the retrieved candidates. This semi-bandit feedback differs from settings where every prediction is followed by the true answer, and it complicates the task of dynamically calibrating prediction sets without a large pre-existing calibration collection.

The authors propose an algorithm for this setting and prove sublinear regret relative to the optimal conformal predictor. This means its cumulative regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so average regret diminishes with continued interaction under the analyzed setup. Evaluations on retrieval, image classification, and auction price-setting report good performance against several baselines, supporting the approach across different applications of incomplete feedback.
icml-2025-stochastic-online-conformal-pr.tldr: A new online conformal algorithm achieves sublinear regret when true labels are observed only if they fall inside its prediction sets.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning lets devices exchange information directly while learning from their separate data. Misbehaving, or Byzantine, devices can disrupt this collaboration. This paper introduces F-RG, a framework for constructing robust decentralized algorithms whose guarantees derive from the aggregation rule used to combine communicated information.

The authors analyze the breakdown point, which describes how much adversarial participation an algorithm can tolerate. They establish an upper bound on the number of adversaries tolerable by decentralized algorithms, then propose a practical aggregation rule called CS+. Using this rule within the framework gives CS+-RG a near-optimal breakdown point. Other aggregation choices recover existing algorithms, including ClippedGossip and NNA.

Experiments support the effectiveness of CS+-RG and reveal a performance gap relative to NNA, particularly under a new attack designed for decentralized communication. The framework thus connects a general tolerance limit, a practical rule approaching that limit, and existing methods within one analysis. Its contribution clarifies how the choice of aggregation mechanism affects resistance to malicious participants in peer-to-peer learning.
icml-2025-unified-breakdown-analysis-for.tldr: F-RG unifies robust decentralized learning algorithms and introduces CS+-RG, which approaches the theoretical limit on tolerated adversarial participation.

paragraphs: A prediction set can meet its coverage target yet remain too large to be informative. This paper studies formal guarantees on set volume in conformal prediction. It first proves an impossibility result for unrestricted distribution-free volume optimality, then changes the objective by limiting the family of prediction sets under consideration.

The main construction uses unions of k intervals, a structured family with finite VC-dimension. An efficient dynamic-programming algorithm finds a set whose volume is near-optimal among unions of k intervals satisfying the desired coverage property, for any distribution. The restriction is central: the comparison is against other sets in the same family, making a meaningful volume guarantee possible.

The authors also extend the conformity score through distributional conformal prediction. With a reasonable estimator of the conditional cumulative distribution function, this supports approximate conditional coverage and conditional restricted volume optimality. Experiments show substantial improvements over existing methods in many settings. The results connect informative set size with explicit structural choices, while keeping the conditional claims dependent on the stated estimation requirement.
icml-2025-volume-optimality-in-conformal.tldr: Restricting prediction sets to unions of k intervals enables efficient, distribution-free near-optimal volume guarantees that are unavailable without such structure.
